analysis.one_liner: Makes private equity firms legally responsible for the debts and harms of companies they buy, and restricts how they extract profits.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a hearing or vote: it was referred to four House committees on the day it was introduced in October 2024 and died when the Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would change the rules for private investment funds that buy controlling stakes in companies. It would make those funds legally liable for the debts, pension obligations, and legal penalties of companies they take over, limit their ability to load companies with debt and pay themselves dividends, give workers higher priority for unpaid wages and severance in bankruptcy, close tax breaks such as the carried-interest tax treatment for fund managers, and bar companies from permanently replacing striking workers. It was introduced with only Democratic support and never moved in any committee.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers at companies owned by private equity funds — the bill's findings say nearly 12 million people work for such companies [S2] — as well as retirees whose pensions are at stake when a portfolio company fails, small creditors, gift-card holders, and pension funds that invest in these funds and currently cannot see fee and performance data [S2].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Workers and retirees at PE-owned firms

how_it_helps.text: Makes controlling private funds jointly and severally liable for the debts, pension withdrawal liabilities, and legal penalties of companies they acquire, so the fund — not just the emptied-out company — pays when an investment fails [S2].

Bars portfolio companies from paying dividends, buybacks, or other capital distributions for four years after a buyout, and caps later distributions, so money cannot be stripped out before a collapse [S2].

Raises the priority of unpaid wages and benefits in bankruptcy to $20,000 per employee, makes promised severance pay a priority claim, and lets back-pay and labor-law penalties be paid as administrative expenses ahead of other creditors [S2].
Restricts bankruptcy bonuses and retention pay for executives, and requires bankruptcy courts to weigh which buyer would best preserve jobs and wages when selling a company's assets [S2].

Ends the special low tax rate on carried interest — the share of investment profits that fund managers receive — by taxing it as ordinary income, and adds a surtax on payments made by controlled companies to investment firms [S2].
Requires funds to disclose fees and returns, imposes fiduciary duties, and lets investors see how private credit deals are marketed, addressing the secrecy the bill's findings describe [S2].
Makes it an unfair labor practice for an employer to permanently replace workers who strike or to lock them out before a strike, reversing current law that allows permanent replacements [S2].

Bars federal health program payments to providers that sell their buildings to or borrow against them with real estate investment trusts, a common financing step in private equity nursing home deals [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Private equity firms and their managers, who would bear liability for portfolio company debts, face a 100-percent-plus surtax structure on payments extracted from controlled companies, lose carried-interest tax treatment and interest deductions, and face disclosure obligations; healthcare REITs lose a special tax rule; and institutional investors such as pension funds that benefit from private equity returns would face reduced access to a leveraged, high-fee investment class.
analysis.who_pays_short: Private equity firms and fund managers

drawbacks.text: Joint and several liability for all debts and liabilities of acquired firms would likely make lenders and insurers far less willing to finance or insure buyouts, which could mean fewer rescue investments in struggling companies — the very cases the bill says it wants to help [S2].

The four-year ban on capital distributions and the surtax on payments from controlled companies could push private capital away from American companies or into structures designed to avoid the rules, which the bill itself tries to head off with anti-evasion provisions [S2].

Institutional investors, including public pension funds that are major private equity investors, would bear part of the cost through reduced returns and restricted fund choices; the bill exempts passive pension fund investors from personal liability but does not shield their returns [S2].

Supporters of the private equity model argue leveraged buyouts also turn around underperforming companies and deliver pension returns, and that the bill's blanket restrictions apply to all control acquisitions, not just failed ones [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill targets a real, documented pattern — its own findings list retail bankruptcies such as Sears, Toys "R" Us, and Payless, and note funds targeting nursing homes, affordable housing, and payday lenders [S2] — and its worker-protection, bankruptcy-priority, and disclosure provisions are the strongest parts. But it is a very broad instrument: unlimited liability for fund investors and a surtax on most payments out of controlled companies would reshape the whole buyout industry, and the costs to credit availability and pension fund returns are real and hard to quantify. The most targeted pieces (bankruptcy priorities, disclosure, the REIT-health provision) are easier to defend than the liability provisions.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to four House committees on the day it was introduced, none of them ever acted on it, and it expired when the Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Rep. Mark Pocan introduced the Stop Wall Street Looting Act on October 11, 2024, with 10 Democratic cosponsors [S1].

The same day, it was referred to four committees — Ways and Means, Financial Services, Judiciary, and Education and the Workforce — meaning any part of it could have been considered by any of them [S4].
No committee held a hearing, marked it up, or reported it out; the only action in its history is the introduction and referral [S4].
The bill died when the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025, and all bills not passed lapse [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Private equity firms and their managers, whose liability, dividend extraction, carried-interest tax treatment, and disclosure practices are all unchanged. Healthcare REITs also keep the tax rule the bill would have repealed.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Private equity firms and fund managers

sides.party_line_note: All 11 sponsors and cosponsors were Democrats, with no Republican support on a bill aimed squarely at the private equity industry, and committee action was controlled by the Republican House majority.

industries.industry: Private equity and private investment funds
industries.note: The bill imposes unlimited liability for portfolio company debts and pensions, bars dividend extraction for four years after a buyout, and adds a surtax on payments from controlled companies — directly cutting into the fee, dividend, and financial-engineering profits the bill's findings describe [S2].
Sections 402 and 403 tax investment services partnership interests as ordinary income rather than at capital gains rates, ending the carried-interest break worth billions to fund managers [S2].

The bill bars federal health program payments to providers that sell or pledge assets to REITs and repeals the special REIT tax rule for healthcare property, cutting off a financing model used in nursing home and hospital deals [S2].
Risk retention requirements for securitized corporate debt and disclosure rules for private credit would reduce fee income and restrict the market for risky corporate loans [S2].

industries.industry: Public and private pension funds investing in private equity
industries.note: Pension funds are explicitly exempted from personal liability as passive investors, but they would lose access to some fund structures and the high returns the private equity industry markets to them, in exchange for fee and performance transparency [S2].
